name: Van Den Broeck Warp Drive
description: Alcubierre's warp bubble with the space inside it expanded by a large factor, so that a bubble microscopic from outside opens through a narrow neck onto a pocket large enough for a ship. Shrinking the bubble's surface brings the negative energy it needs from far beyond the mass of the visible universe down to a few solar masses.
history: How small can a warp drive look from outside and still carry a ship? Michael Pfenning and Lawrence Ford found in 1997 that the wall of an Alcubierre bubble can be no thicker than about a hundred Planck lengths at speeds near that of light [pfenning1997]. Their tool was the quantum inequality of Ford and Thomas Roman: an observer can see a large negative energy density only for a short time, and the more negative it is, the shorter the time [ford1996]. A bubble 100 m in radius with so thin a wall needs at least $-6.2\times10^{62}\,v_s$ kg of negative energy, which they put at ten orders of magnitude beyond the mass of the visible universe [pfenning1997]. They also remarked that a bubble far smaller than an atom needs much less: one with the radius of an electron's Compton wavelength takes about 400 solar masses [pfenning1997].¶Chris Van Den Broeck built a drive out of that remark in May 1999 [vandenbroeck1999]. His plan was to keep "the surface area of the warp bubble itself microscopically small, while at the same time expanding the spatial volume inside the bubble" [vandenbroeck1999]. He multiplied the space of Alcubierre's metric by $B^2(r_s)$, a function of the distance $r_s$ from the ship equal to $1 + \alpha$ near it and to $1$ from a little farther out, with $\alpha$ very large [vandenbroeck1999]. He pictured a slice of it as a rubber membrane: "A small Alcubierre bubble surrounds a neck leading to a 'pocket' with a large internal volume, with a flat region in the middle" [vandenbroeck1999]. The ship rides in that flat region on a timelike geodesic, and its clock keeps the coordinate time $t$ [vandenbroeck1999].¶His example has $\alpha = 10^{17}$, a pocket of coordinate radius $\tilde{R} = 10^{-15}$ m, a neck of the same thickness, and a bubble wall beginning at $R = 3\times10^{-15}$ m [vandenbroeck1999]. From outside the bubble is a few femtometres across, and the pocket inside it measures 200 m from wall to wall: it is bigger on the inside [vandenbroeck1999]. The wall holds about $-6.3\times10^{29}\,v_s$ kg, and the neck holds $-1.4\times10^{30}$ kg of negative energy next to $+4.9\times10^{30}$ kg of positive, each a few solar masses [vandenbroeck1999]. In his words, that "puts the warp drive in the mass scale of large traversable wormholes" [vandenbroeck1999].¶Sines and low order polynomials for $B$ gave him curvature radii far below the Planck length, so across the neck he took a polynomial of degree 80 with many derivatives vanishing where the neck meets flat space [vandenbroeck1999]. He picked 80 because it makes the smallest curvature radius as large as it can be, $1.4\times10^{-34}$ m, about ten Planck lengths [vandenbroeck1999]. The energy density in the neck reaches $-6.6\times10^{93}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, inside the quantum inequality's bound of $-9.2\times10^{94}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ [vandenbroeck1999]. He called the result a "proof of principle" and said the proposal is not realistic, since the energy densities remain unreasonably large and the geometry has structure only a few orders of magnitude above the Planck scale [vandenbroeck1999].¶In June 1999 Van Den Broeck reviewed the objections to Alcubierre's drive [vandenbroeck1999b]. The energy problem he counted as "partially solved" [vandenbroeck1999b]. The feature he judged most problematic was one Serguei Krasnikov and D. H. Coule had raised: in a bubble faster than light, part of the exotic matter in the wall has to move faster than light itself [vandenbroeck1999b, krasnikov1998, coule1998]. He concluded that "superluminal warp bubbles seem an unlikely possibility" within general relativity and quantum field theory, "although subluminal bubbles may still be possible" [vandenbroeck1999b].¶The pocket fits other shortcuts too, and Krasnikov took it up in 2003 under the heading "Van Den Broeck's trick" [krasnikov2003]. He wrote it in the proper distance $l$ along a radius, $ds^2 = -dt^2 + dl^2 + r(l)^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$, the line element of Morris and Thorne's wormhole closed off at a centre where $r = 0$, and took $r(l)$ quadratic through the neck [krasnikov2003]. His pocket needs about a milligram of exotic matter, and by his estimate Van Den Broeck's polynomial takes $10^{36}$ times more and breaks the quantum inequality near the inner end of the neck [krasnikov2003]. The Krasnikov tube takes the same treatment, which is how Pierre Gravel and Jean-Luc Plante lowered its mass in 2004 [gravel2004, lobo2004]. A bubble whose inside is stretched along the direction of travel alone is Alexey Bobrick and Gianni Martire's version of 2021 [bobrick2021].

related.text: Van Den Broeck's drive with $B = 1$ everywhere. Every slice of Alcubierre's bubble is flat, and Van Den Broeck's has a pocket curved into it [vandenbroeck1999].
The other shortcut built from negative energy. Pierre Gravel and Jean-Luc Plante lowered the mass of the tube in 2004 in the spirit of Van Den Broeck's pocket [gravel2004, lobo2004].

In the proper distance $l$ the pocket is Morris and Thorne's line element with $\Phi = 0$, closed off at a centre where $r = 0$, so its neck is a wormhole throat that opens onto a room [krasnikov2003].

coordinates.name: Cartesian

parameters.description: Bubble velocity in units of $c$, a function of $t$ alone. The centre of the pocket follows the world line $x = x_s(t)$ with $dx_s/dt = c\,v_s(t)$, a timelike geodesic whose proper time is $t$, and $v_s > 1$ is allowed. Van Den Broeck takes $v_s$ constant for his estimates. The prime is the derivative along the chart coordinate, $v_s' = dv_s/d(ct)$, so it carries an inverse length.

Alcubierre's shape function, dimensionless, here an arbitrary function of the four coordinates. Van Den Broeck takes a function of $r_s = \sqrt{(x - x_s(t))^2 + y^2 + z^2}$, the coordinate distance from the centre, with $f = 1$ for $r_s < R$, $0 < f \le 1$ across the wall $R \le r_s < R + \Delta$, and $f = 0$ for $r_s \ge R + \Delta$. No component needs that choice, and none assumes $\partial_t f = -v_s\,\partial_x f$.

Expansion factor of space, dimensionless, here an arbitrary function of the four coordinates. Van Den Broeck takes a twice differentiable function of $r_s$ with $B = 1 + \alpha$ in the pocket $r_s < \tilde{R}$, $1 < B \le 1 + \alpha$ across the neck $\tilde{R} \le r_s < \tilde{R} + \tilde{\Delta}$, and $B = 1$ for $r_s \ge \tilde{R} + \tilde{\Delta}$, with $R > \tilde{R} + \tilde{\Delta}$, so the neck sits inside the wall of the bubble. Every length inside the pocket is $1 + \alpha$ times its coordinate length. Where $B = 1$ the metric is Alcubierre's.

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths. The velocity $v_s$ of the bubble is in units of $c$, and the shape function $f$ and the expansion factor $B$ are dimensionless functions of all four coordinates. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, where $\partial_t = c^{-1}\partial/\partial t$ and $v_s' = dv_s/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Comoving Spherical

parameters.description: Expansion factor of space, dimensionless, a function of $r$ alone. It is $1 + \alpha$, for a large number $\alpha$, in the pocket $r < \tilde{R}$, falls across the neck $\tilde{R} \le r < \tilde{R} + \tilde{\Delta}$, and is $1$ from there out to the wall of the bubble at $r = R$. Van Den Broeck's choice across the neck is $B = 1 + \alpha\left(n\,w^{n-1} - (n - 1)\,w^n\right)$ with $w = (\tilde{R} + \tilde{\Delta} - r)/\tilde{\Delta}$ and $n = 80$. A sphere of coordinate radius $r$ has area $4\pi B^2r^2$.
Coordinate radius at which the wall of the bubble begins, a length. Inside it $f = 1$, and Van Den Broeck's example has $R = 3\times10^{-15}$ m.

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ centred on the ship, with $x - x_s(t) = r\cos\theta$, $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and $r$ a length. The chart covers the inside of the bubble, where $f = 1$, and the expansion factor $B$ is a dimensionless function of $r$ alone. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is a derivative with respect to $r$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

domains: l = -l_0 \;\text{(the centre of the pocket, where } r = 0\text{)}

parameters.description: Areal radius of the sphere at proper distance $l$, a length, so that the sphere has area $4\pi r^2$. It vanishes at the centre of the pocket, grows to the pocket's full radius, shrinks through the neck to a minimum, and grows again as $r = l$ plus a constant outside. In the comoving spherical chart, whose radius we call $\rho$ here, $dl = B\,d\rho$ and $r = B\rho$. A prime is a derivative with respect to $l$.
Proper distance from the centre of the pocket to the sphere $l = 0$ in the neck, a length. Krasnikov puts $l = 0$ at the middle of the layer where $r'' > 0$.

The areal radius $r$ is a function of $l$ alone, and the chart covers the inside of the bubble, where $f = 1$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is a derivative with respect to $l$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
